strengths: The paper achieves outstanding empirical performance, demonstrating an approximate 5x training speedup (80% compute savings) on models up to 7B parameters with negligible loss degradation.

The proposed zero/one-layer progressive training framework is remarkably simple, practical, and elegant. It eliminates the need for complex layer-ordering, interpolation, or multi-stage progressive scheduling used in previous work.

The paper provides a thorough theoretical and analytical foundation, connecting progressive training to feature learning (muP) and optimization (projected gradient descent). It explains why the Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule is uniquely suited for progressive training.

The experimental evaluation is highly comprehensive, covering over 150 runs across three different model families (GPT2, MoE, and ResNet) and extensively investigating multiple hyperparameter transfer strategies, initialization types, and optimizer states.
weaknesses: The convergence analysis in Section 4 relies on a convex and G-Lipschitz assumption. While the authors motivate why deep learning behaves similarly, the theory remains simplified and does not fully address non-convex phenomena, such as how the model navigates different basins of attraction after a massive depth expansion.

The definition of a 'zero-layer' model (specifically for the Transformer architecture) could be made more explicit in the main body of the text. While it is implied to consist of only the embeddings and the output projection head, a clear definition would prevent initial reader confusion.

The 7B parameter scaling experiments are primarily compared against the fixed-size baseline. Including at least one competitive progressive training baseline (e.g., standard stacking or ELLE) at this scale would make the comparative advantage even more convincing, although the smaller-scale experiments already show the limitations of those methods.

strengths: The paper proposes an incredibly simple yet highly effective progressive training scheme (zero/one-layer depth expansion) that achieves remarkable compute savings (up to 80% or 5x speedup) on models up to 7B parameters.
Comprehensive empirical analysis across different architectures (GPT2, Mixture of Experts, and ResNet) and model sizes, demonstrating consistent "mixing" behaviors.

The paper provides deep insights into the critical role of the learning rate schedule, demonstrating why the Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule is vastly superior to the cosine decay schedule for enabling late-stage depth expansion (up to 80% of the training horizon).
The work connects progressive training to maximal update parametrization (muP) to ensure feature learning and allow zero-shot hyperparameter transfer.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, structured, and easy to follow, with clear "Takeaway" boxes summarizing key lessons for practitioners.
weaknesses: The 7B model is trained on OpenWebText for only 600k iterations with a small batch size, which corresponds to a very small token budget (a few billion tokens). This is highly undertrained for a 7B model. It remains unproven whether the ~5x speedup and mixing behaviors still hold when training on trillions of tokens to compute-optimality.

The theoretical convergence analysis in Section 4 relies on highly simplified assumptions of convexity and G-Lipschitz continuity of the loss function, which do not capture the non-convex dynamics of deep neural networks.

The evaluation is primarily focused on pre-training validation loss. A more comprehensive evaluation including downstream zero-shot or fine-tuning performance on standard benchmarks would strengthen the paper's claims.

strengths: Outstanding empirical thoroughness, with over 150 training runs analyzing different configurations, target model depths, and hyperparameters.
Demonstrates highly impressive compute savings (up to 5x speedup) on large-scale models, including a 7B parameter GPT-2 model trained on OpenWebText.
The concept of zero/one-layer depth expansion is simple, elegant, and avoids the complex layer-ordering and interpolation issues of prior progressive training methods.
Provides a comprehensive ablation study covering learning rate schedules (Cosine vs. WSD), optimizer states, batch sizes, and model architectures (dense GPT-2, ResNet, MoE).
Attempts to bridge empirical findings with optimization theory, offering a PGD-based perspective that successfully motivates the use of the WSD schedule.
weaknesses: The evaluation on the 7B model uses a relatively small token budget (~39B tokens), which means the target model is highly undertrained. In standard, compute-optimal, or overtrained regimes (e.g., training a 7B model on 2T+ tokens), a 0-layer model would saturate its capacity extremely early. Spending 80% of the token budget on a 0-layer model would leave the full 60-layer model with only 20% of the tokens, which may not be sufficient to train the deep transformer blocks to the same level of performance as a fixed-size model trained on the full token budget.

The 0-layer model lacks any transformer blocks and behaves essentially as a bag-of-words or bigram model. Training this architecture for 80% of the training run prevents the model from learning any deep hierarchical representations or long-range contextual dependencies until the very end of the training process. While the embeddings and language model head get highly optimized, this extreme delay in learning contextual representations might hurt downstream performance on complex reasoning or long-context tasks, which is not fully captured by validation perplexity alone.

The theoretical convergence analysis in Section 4 makes the highly simplifying assumption of a convex and G-Lipschitz loss. While this is a standard starting point for optimization theory, transformer training is highly non-convex and exhibits complex feature learning dynamics. Consequently, the theoretical insights provide a loose qualitative analogy rather than a rigorous guarantee for the behavior of deep transformers.

The progressive training recipe heavily relies on Muon-NSGD to achieve its best results. While the authors show some experiments with AdamW, the massive speedup and clean mixing behaviors seem to be enhanced by Muon's optimization properties. This dependency could limit the immediate applicability of the method in standard industrial pipelines that rely strictly on AdamW.
